title: Clopidogrel versus low‐dose aspirin as risk factors for epistaxis

sections.abstract: <jats:p><jats:bold>Objectives: </jats:bold> To quantify the relative risk of epistaxis for patients taking low‐dose aspirin or clopidogrel compared to patients taking neither drug.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Design: </jats:bold> Case‐control study.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Setting: </jats:bold> Primary care.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Participants: </jats:bold> 10,241 patients from three GP practices in the West Midlands.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Main outcome measures: </jats:bold> Epistaxis resulting in presentation to the GP, attendance at Accident & Emergency, or referral to ENT outpatients.</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Results: </jats:bold> There was a significant difference in the proportion of patients with epistaxis across the three groups (<jats:italic>χ</jats:italic><jats:sup>2</jats:sup> = 84.1; 2 degrees of freedom; <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.000001). Relative risk of epistaxis was increased in both the aspirin (RR = 9.04; 95% CI = 5.13–15.96) and clopidogrel (RR = 6.40; 95% CI = 2.33–17.56) groups compared to the no drug group. There was no increased risk of epistaxis with aspirin compared to clopidogrel (RR = 1.4; 95% CI = 0.6–3.4).</jats:p><jats:p><jats:bold>Conclusion: </jats:bold> There is an increased risk of troublesome epistaxis in patients taking aspirin or clopidogrel. There is no significant difference in risk of epistaxis between the two drug groups.</jats:p>
